flawed_step: Step 3: The proof would need to infer from planarity that some two-color component contains every neighboring occurrence of one color and no neighboring occurrence of the other. Planarity does not guarantee such a favorable Kempe component.
counterexample: Let V(G)={v,a1,b,a2,c,d}. Join v to all five other vertices. In G-v, use the outer cycle a1-b-a2-c-d-a1 and add chords b-c and b-d. This is planar: draw the two chords as a noncrossing fan from b inside the cycle and draw v with its five incident edges on the other side. Color a1=a2=1, b=2, c=3, d=4. This is proper, and N(v) uses all four colors. The Kempe components are: for colors 1,2, the single component {a1,b,a2}; for 1,3, the components {a1} and {a2,c}; for 1,4, the components {a2} and {a1,d}; and for 2,3, 2,4, and 3,4, respectively the single components {b,c}, {b,d}, and {c,d}. Swapping the 1,2 component merely exchanges colors 1 and 2 on those neighbors. Each 1,3 or 1,4 swap leaves another occurrence of color 1 or exchanges both represented colors. Each of the remaining swaps exchanges two singleton neighbor colors. Thus every possible single Kempe-chain interchange leaves all four colors on N(v), so the coloring cannot be extended to v after one interchange.
assessment_summary: A proof attempt reaches the necessary Kempe-chain existence claim but cannot justify it from planarity. The explicit six-vertex planar graph above shows that every possible interchange preserves all four neighbor colors, directly falsifying the statement.
